Non-GAAP Financial Measures

Adjusted OIBDA and Adjusted OIBDA margin are financial measures that are not calculated in accordance with GAAP in the United States. Adjusted OIBDA represents operating income before depreciation and amortization expense adjusted to also exclude non-cash share-based compensation costs, workforce and system transformation costs, satellite transition costs, acquisition and integration costs and advisor fees related to involvement in Regal’s Chapter 11 case (the “Cineworld Proceeding”) and NCM LLC's Chapter 11 Case (the “Chapter 11 Case”). Adjusted OIBDA margin is calculated by dividing Adjusted OIBDA by total revenue. Our management uses these non-GAAP financial measures to evaluate operating performance, to forecast future results and as a basis for compensation. The Company believes these are important supplemental measures of operating performance because they eliminate items that have less bearing on its operating performance and highlight trends in its core business that may not otherwise be apparent when relying solely on GAAP financial measures. The Company believes the presentation of these measures is relevant and useful for investors because it enables them to view performance in a manner similar to the method used by the Company’s management, improves their ability to understand the Company’s operating performance and makes it easier to compare the Company’s results with other companies that may have different depreciation and amortization policies, non-cash share-based compensation programs, workforce and system transformation costs, satellite transition costs, acquisition and integration costs and advisor fees related to involvement in the Cineworld Proceeding and Chapter 11 Case, interest rates, debt levels or income tax rates. A limitation of these measures, however, is that they exclude depreciation and amortization, which represent a proxy for the periodic costs of certain capitalized tangible and intangible assets used in generating revenues in the Company’s business. In addition, Adjusted OIBDA has the limitation of not reflecting the effect of the Company’s share-based payment costs, workforce and system transformation costs, satellite transition costs, acquisition and integration costs and advisor fees related to involvement in the Cineworld Proceeding and Chapter 11 Case. Adjusted OIBDA should not be regarded as an alternative to operating income, net income or as indicators of operating performance, nor should it be considered in isolation of, or as substitutes for financial measures prepared in accordance with GAAP. The Company believes that operating income is the most directly comparable GAAP financial measure to Adjusted OIBDA, and operating margin is the most directly comparable GAAP financial measure to Adjusted OIBDA margin. Because not all companies use identical calculations, these non-GAAP presentations may not be comparable to other similarly titled measures of other companies or calculations in the Company’s debt agreement.

Cinema advertising revenue. Cinema advertising revenue decreased by $4.2 million, or 7.1%, from $59.5 million for the third quarter of 2025 to $55.3 million for the third quarter of 2026. The decrease was primarily due to a $3.8 million decrease in national cinema advertising revenue, as well as a $0.5 million decrease in local and regional cinema advertising revenue. The decrease in national cinema advertising revenue was primarily due to a 16.3% decrease in utilization and a 3.7% decrease in CPMs. The national cinema advertising revenue decrease was partially offset by a 24.3% increase in network attendance in the third quarter of 2026, as compared to the third quarter of 2025. The decrease in local and regional cinema advertising revenue was driven by a $1.8 million film specific campaign in the entertainment category in the third quarter of 2025, without corresponding activity in the third quarter of 2026. The local and regional cinema advertising revenue decrease was partially offset by an increase in the contract activity and the size within the retail and apparel, finance, dining and gaming categories in the third quarter of 2026, as compared to the third quarter of 2025.

Office/residential advertising revenue. Office/Residential advertising revenue increased by $2.2 million, or 100%, from $0.0 million for the third quarter of 2025 to $2.2 million for the third quarter of 2026. The increase in office/residential advertising revenue was due to completion of the acquisition of Captivate on September 18, 2026, with the balance representing activity from September 19, 2026 through October 1, 2026.

Other revenue. Other revenue remained consistent at $3.9 million for the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026. The decrease in other revenue was primarily due to a $0.3 million decrease in ESA Party beverage revenue caused by a decrease in the amount of the onscreen advertising purchased by an ESA party in accordance with its underlying beverage concessionaire agreement in the third quarter of 2026, as compared to the third quarter of 2025. This decrease was partially offset by a 14.7% increase in ESA Party attendance in the third quarter of 2026, as compared to the third quarter of 2025. This decrease was also offset by other revenue from Captivate of $0.3 million, representing activity from September 19, 2026 through October 1, 2026, in the third quarter of 2026, subsequent to the acquisition on September 18, 2026.

Operating expenses. Total operating expenses increased $17.8 million, or 27.3%, from $65.2 million for the third quarter of 2025 to $83.0 million for the third quarter of 2026. Network operating costs. Network operating costs remained consistent at $3.2 million for the third quarter of 2026 and the third quarter of 2025. There was a $0.6 million decrease in personnel expenses related to the 2026 Transformation Initiative. This decrease was partially offset by a $0.2 million increase in satellite testing expenses and a $0.1 million increase in annual licensing costs in the third quarter of 2026, as compared to the third quarter of 2025. The decrease was also partially offset by $0.3 million in expenses related to Captivate's operating results from September 19, 2026 through October 1, 2026.

Theater exhibition fees. Theater exhibition fees increased by $7.9 million, or 24.5%, from $32.3 million for the third quarter of 2025 to $40.2 million for the third quarter of 2026. The increase was primarily related to a $6.2 million increase due to the 24.3% increase in network attendance partially driven by the acquisition of Spotlight, a $1.1 million increase driven by contractual rate increases within and renegotiations of our exhibitor agreements and a $0.6 million increase corresponding to the increase in platinum revenue in the third quarter of 2026, as compared to the third quarter of 2025.

Selling and marketing costs. Selling and marketing costs decreased $1.1 million, or 10.9%, from $10.1 million for the third quarter of 2025 to $9.0 million for the third quarter of 2026. The decrease was primarily related to a $0.8 million decrease in selling related expenses due to the 2026 Transformation Initiative, primarily caused by the cancellation of certain contracts, a $0.6 million decrease in performance related compensation correlating to the decrease in revenue, a $0.5 million decrease in personnel related costs due to the 2026 Transformation Initiative and a $0.3 million decrease in bad debt expense for the third quarter of 2026 compared to the third quarter of 2025. These decreases were partially offset by $0.8 million in expense attributable to Captivate’s operating activity following its consolidation on September 19, 2026 through October 1, 2026 and a $0.2 million increase in variable partnership costs in the third quarter of 2026, as compared to the third quarter of 2025.

Administrative and other costs. Administrative and other costs increased $8.9 million, or 84.0%, from $10.6 million for the third quarter of 2025 to $19.5 million for the third quarter of 2026. The increase was primarily related to $8.9 million in legal and professional expenses incurred in connection with completion of the Captivate Acquisition, $1.5 million in bad debt expense incurred to establish Captivate's allowance for credit losses in accordance with ASC 805, $0.6 million in expenses attributable to Captivate’s operating activity following its consolidation on September 19, 2026 through October 1, 2026 and a $0.5 million increase in share-based compensation expense for the third quarter of 2026 compared to the third quarter of 2025. These increases were partially offset by a $1.2 million decrease in bonus expenses due to the Company's projected performance as compared to compensation targets, a $0.6 million decrease in legal and professional fees related to activity in the prior year not incurred in the current year, in part due to the 2026 Transformation Initiative, and a $0.6 million decrease in personnel related costs, a $0.2 million decrease in lease expense and a $0.2 million decrease in cloud computing costs driven by the 2026 Transformation Initiative for the third quarter of 2026 compared to the third quarter of 2025.

Depreciation expense. Depreciation expense increased $0.5 million, or 45.5%, from $1.1 million for the third quarter of 2025, to $1.6 million for the third quarter of 2026. The increase was primarily due to assets placed in service in late 2025 related to the completion of certain leasehold improvements as well as $0.1 million in expense attributable to Captivate’s operating activity following its consolidation on September 19, 2026 through October 1, 2026.

Amortization expense. Amortization expense increased $1.0 million, or 12.7%, from $7.9 million for the third quarter of 2025 to $8.9 million for the third quarter of 2026. The increase was primarily due to $1.0 million in amortization related to intangible assets recognized in conjunction with completion of the acquisition of Captivate on September 18, 2026.

Goodwill impairment. Goodwill impairment increased $0.6 million, or 100.0%, from $0.0 million for the third quarter of 2025 to $0.6 million for the third quarter of 2026. The increase was due to the $0.6 million impairment of the goodwill under the NCM LLC reporting unit in the third quarter of 2026.

Known Trends and Uncertainties

Beverage revenue—Under the ESAs, up to 90 seconds of The Noovie® Show program can be sold to the ESA Parties to satisfy their on-screen advertising commitments under their beverage concessionaire agreements. In 2025, one ESA party purchased 60 seconds of on-screen advertising time and one ESA party purchased 30 seconds to satisfy their obligations under their beverage concessionaire agreements. In 2026, one ESA party began purchasing less on-screen advertising time for nine months of the year in accordance with its beverage concessionaire agreement. This change in the ESA party's obligation will result in lower beverage revenue in 2026, as compared to 2025. The price for the time sold will increase at a fixed rate of 2.0% each year. Beverage revenue is included within ‘Other revenue’ within the disaggregation of revenue table presented within Note 2—Revenue from contracts with customers and accounts receivable.

Theater exhibition fees—In consideration for the Company’s access to the ESA Parties’ and network affiliate theaters for on-screen and LEN advertising and lobby promotions, the ESA Parties and network affiliates receive access fees based either upon number of attendees, a revenue share or a combination, including a minimum revenue guarantee per attendee. Many of these

 

32

 

agreements contain annual increases to the respective fee structures or guaranteed minimums, either per patron, per theater and/or per digital screen. In May 2026, the Company implemented changes in the fee structure of an ESA party's beverage agreement which will result in increased theater exhibition fees in 2026, as compared to 2025. The payments under the ESA Parties' agreements and network affiliate agreements are recorded within ‘Theater exhibition fees’ in the unaudited Condensed Consolidated Statements of Operations.

Financial Condition and Liquidity

Liquidity and Capital Resources

Our cash balances can fluctuate due to the seasonality of our business and related timing of collections of accounts receivable balances and operating expenditure payments, as well as interest and principal payments on our 2026 Credit Facilities, if any, income tax payments, TRA payments to Cinemark and available cash payments (as defined in the NCM LLC Operating Agreement) to Cinemark in the event Cinemark holds NCM LLC membership units, as well as the amount of dividends paid to NCM, Inc.’s common stockholders.

On September 18, 2026, NCM Holdings, together with NCM LLC and Captivate, as borrowers, entered into the 2026 Credit Agreement. The 2026 Credit Agreement provides for a $275.0 million senior secured first lien term loan and for a $25.0 million revolving credit facility that both mature on September 18, 2031. In connection with entering into the 2026 Credit Agreement, NCM LLC repaid in full the $12.0 million balance outstanding and terminated all commitments under its 2025 Credit Facility. As of October 1, 2026, NCM Holdings had an outstanding balance of $275.0 million under the 2026 Term Loan Facility and $10.0 million outstanding under the 2026 Revolving Facility. Borrowings under the 2026 Revolving Facility may be used for, among other things, working capital and other general corporate purposes of the Company. The 2026 Credit Agreement bears interest at a margin over a reference rate selected at the option of the borrower. The margin for the 2026 Credit Agreement is 7.00% per annum for SOFR borrowings and 6.00% per annum for base rate borrowings.

Sources of Capital and Capital Requirements

NCM, Inc.’s primary source of liquidity and capital resources is the quarterly available cash distributions from NCM LLC (as allowed for under the 2026 Revolving Credit Facility) as well as existing cash balances within its subsidiaries, NCM LLC and Captivate, which as of October 1, 2026, were $27.8 million (including $19.3 million and $2.4 million of cash held by NCM LLC and Captivate, respectively). NCM LLC and Captivate’s primary sources of liquidity and capital resources are cash provided by their respective operating activities, availability under the 2026 Revolving Credit Facility and cash on hand. The $19.3 million of cash at NCM LLC and the $2.4 million of cash at Captivate will be used to fund operations and strategic investments.

NCM, Inc. expects to use its cash balances and cash received from future available cash distributions (as allowed for under the 2026 Revolving Credit Facility) to fund income taxes, payments associated with the TRA, stock repurchases and future dividends if and when declared by the Board of Directors. The Company made an estimated TRA payment in 2026 for the 2025 tax year and made an estimated TRA payment in 2025 for the 2024 tax year. Deferred distributions from NCM LLC and NCM, Inc. cash balances should be sufficient to fund payments associated with the TRA, income taxes and any stock repurchases or declared dividends for the foreseeable future. At the discretion of the Board of Directors, the Company will consider returning a portion of its free cash flow to stockholders. The declaration, payment, timing and amount of any future stock repurchases or dividends payable will be at the sole discretion of the Board of Directors who will take into account general economic and advertising market business conditions, restrictions in the 2026 Credit Agreement, the Company’s financial condition, available cash, current and anticipated cash needs and any other factors that the Board of Directors considers relevant.

Critical Accounting Policies

Captivate Acquisition—The Company accounted for the acquisition of Captivate using the acquisition method of accounting. The acquisition method requires the Company to make significant estimates and assumptions, especially at the acquisition date as the Company allocates the estimated fair values of acquired tangible and intangible assets and the liabilities assumed. The Company also uses our best estimates to determine the useful lives of the tangible and definite-lived intangible assets, which impact the periods over which depreciation and amortization of those assets are recognized. These best estimates and assumptions are inherently uncertain as they pertain to forward looking views of the Company’s businesses, client behavior and market conditions. See Note 4—Business Combinations for further information on the valuation methods utilized and the results of the application of the acquisition method of accounting, including the estimated fair values of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed, and, where relevant, the estimated remaining useful lives. The ongoing accounting for the tangible and intangible assets acquired requires the Company to make significant estimates and assumptions and exercise judgment to evaluate these assets for impairment. The processes and accounting policies for evaluating impairments are further described in Note 1—The Company.

Goodwill—Goodwill is allocated to the reporting unit in which the business that created the goodwill resides. A reporting unit can be an operating segment, or a business unit one level below that operating segment, for which discrete financial information is prepared and regularly reviewed by segment management.

 

34

 

As of October 1, 2026, the Company has concluded that it has two reporting units, NCM LLC and Captivate. As required, the Company evaluates the carrying value of goodwill at the reporting unit level for impairment at least annually or when an interim triggering event occurs that may indicate potential impairment. The Company's annual test is performed as of the first day of the last fiscal month of the year, which in 2026, falls on December 4, 2026. The testing of goodwill uses estimates and assumptions affected by factors such as economic and industry conditions along with changes in forecasted operating performance. The evaluation involves comparing the reporting unit's fair value to its carrying value. If the fair value exceeds its respective carrying value, then the Company concludes that no impairment has occurred. If the carrying value exceeds its fair value, the Company would recognize an impairment loss in an amount equal to the excess up to the total amount of goodwill allocated to that reporting unit.

For further discussion of accounting policies that we consider critical to our business operations and understanding of our results of operations, and that affect the more significant judgments and estimates used in the preparation of our unaudited Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, see Item 7. “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations—Critical Accounting Estimates” contained in our Annual Report on Form 10-K, filed for the fiscal year ended January 1, 2026, and incorporated by reference herein. As of October 1, 2026, there were no other significant changes in those critical accounting policies.

For a discussion of recent accounting pronouncements, see the information provided under Note 1—The Company to the unaudited Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements in Part I, Item 1 of this Form 10-Q.

Item 3. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk

Interest Rate Risk

The primary market risk to which we are exposed is interest rate risk. As of October 1, 2026, the interest rate risk that we are exposed to is related to our $275.0 million term loan and our $25.0 million revolving credit facility, under the 2026 Credit Agreement. A 100-basis point fluctuation in market interest rates underlying our term loan and revolving credit facility would have the effect of increasing or decreasing our cash interest expense by approximately $2.9 million for an annual period on the $275.0 million term loan outstanding and the $10.0 million revolving credit balance as of October 1, 2026.

Foreign Currency Risk

Our financial results may be impacted by foreign currency exchange gains or losses in Canada. As a result, we may experience foreign currency gains or losses, which may positively or negatively affect our results of operations. For the nine months ended October 1, 2026, revenue associated with this foreign exchange risk was less than 1% of our consolidated revenue.

Item 4. Controls and Procedures

The Company maintains disclosure controls and procedures as defined in Rules 13a-15(e) and 15d-15(e) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (the “Exchange Act”), that are designed to ensure that information required to be disclosed in the Company's reports filed under the Exchange Act, is recorded, processed, summarized and reported within the time periods specified by the SEC’s rules and forms, and that such information is accumulated and communicated to management, including the Chief Executive Officer (principal executive officer) and Chief Financial Officer (principal financial and accounting officer), as appropriate, to allow timely decisions regarding required disclosure.

Management, with the participation of the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer, performed an evaluation of the effectiveness of the Company’s disclosure controls and procedures pursuant to Rules 13a-15(e) and 15d-15(e) of the Exchange Act as of October 1, 2026, the end of the period covered by this Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q. Based on such evaluation, the Company’s management concluded that the Company’s disclosure controls and procedures, as of October 1, 2026, were effective.

In designing and evaluating our disclosure controls and procedures, management recognizes that any control, no matter how well designed and operated, can provide only reasonable, not absolute, assurance of achieving the desired control objectives. Due to the inherent limitations in all control systems, no evaluation of controls can provide absolute assurance that misstatements due to error or fraud will not occur or that all control issues and instances of fraud, if any, within the Company have been detected.

Changes in Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

On September 18, 2026, we completed the acquisition of Captivate and have implemented new processes and enhanced existing internal controls to assist us in the preparation and disclosure of financial information. Given the significance of the Captivate Acquisition, we intend to exclude the acquired Captivate business from our assessment and report on internal controls over financial reporting for the year ended December 31, 2026. There were no other changes to our internal control over financial reporting that occurred during the quarter ended October 1, 2026 that have materially affected, or are reasonably likely to materially affect, our internal control over financial reporting.

Item 1A. Risk Factors

Ownership of the common stock and other securities of the Company involves certain risks. You should carefully consider the following material risks and other information in this document, including our historical financial statements and related notes included herein and the risk factors as previously disclosed in our Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q filed with the SEC on May 12, 2026 for the three months ended April 2, 2026 and our Annual Report on Form 10-K filed with the SEC on February 26, 2026 for the fiscal year ended January 1, 2026. The material risks and uncertainties described in our Annual Report on Form 10-K and this document are not the only ones facing us. If any of the risks and uncertainties described in our Annual Report on Form 10-K, our Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the three months ended April 2, 2026 and this document actually occur, our business, financial condition and results of operations could be adversely affected in a material way. This could cause the trading price of our common stock to decline, perhaps significantly, and you may lose part or all of your investment.

Risks Related to the Captivate Acquisition

We may not realize the anticipated benefits of the Captivate Acquisition, including anticipated cost and revenue synergies, within the expected time frame or at all, and integrating Captivate may be more difficult, costly or time-consuming than expected.

On September 18, 2026, NCM Holdings, LLC, our wholly owned subsidiary, completed the acquisition of all of the outstanding equity interests of Captivate Holdings, LLC and Captivate Network Holdings, Inc. (together with their subsidiaries, “Captivate”) for an enterprise value of $275.0 million in cash, subject to customary net working capital and other purchase price adjustments (the “Captivate Acquisition”), pursuant to a Securities Purchase Agreement and Plan of Merger (the “Purchase Agreement”). We financed the Captivate Acquisition with borrowings under the 2026 Credit Facilities and cash on hand.

The success of the Captivate Acquisition will depend on our ability to continue to grow Captivate’s building network and advertising base, and on our ability to realize anticipated benefits from integrating Captivate’s business with our cinema advertising platform. Those benefits include offering advertisers access to a broader premium video platform through both direct and programmatic buying channels; creating incremental, cross-selling opportunities across national and local advertising clients; and achieving anticipated annual run-rate cost synergies. Captivate’s advertising business and growth potential may be adversely affected by digital out of home industry headwinds, such as global sporting events or agency consolidation; changes in office occupancy and utilization, including effects from pandemics or other public health events; and building footprint volatility from third-party managed networks or widespread effects of aging technology infrastructure. Further, the integration process may present material challenges, including:

•
combining sales organizations, sales strategies and advertising products,
•
retaining advertising clients, agency relationships and building owner and property manager relationships during the integration;
•
integrating or consolidating information technology, advertising management, data, measurement and financial reporting systems;
•
eliminating duplicative corporate overhead and consolidating executive and administrative functions without disrupting operations;
•
retaining key employees and managing differing company benefits programs and policies; and
•
the diversion of management’s attention from our core advertising business and other strategic initiatives.

Many of these factors are outside of our control. The integration process is complex and may materially disrupt our sales, finance, human resources, operations, technology, marketing, and executive teams. Even if we successfully integrate Captivate, we may not realize the anticipated synergies or other benefits within the expected time frame, or at all, and the costs of achieving them may exceed our estimates. Our expectations for the Captivate Acquisition were based on assumptions about, among other things, Captivate’s historical growth, office and residential occupancy trends and advertiser demand, which may prove to be inaccurate. If we fail to realize the anticipated benefits, our business, financial condition and results of operations, our ability to service our indebtedness and the market price of our common stock could be adversely affected.

We may be subject to unknown or contingent liabilities of Captivate, and our recourse under the Purchase Agreement is limited.

We purchased the equity of Captivate in the Captivate Acquisition and as a result we assumed all of Captivate’s liabilities, including liabilities that were unknown at the time of the Captivate Acquisition or that we underestimated in our due diligence, such as liabilities related to taxes, employment matters, compliance with law, data privacy and security, intellectual property, and contracts

 

36

 

with building owners, advertisers and vendors. We obtained a representation and warranties insurance policy in connection with the Captivate Acquisition, which is our primary source of recovery for breaches by the sellers and Captivate’s representations and warranties in the Purchase Agreement. The policy is subject to customary exclusions and retention and coverage limits and may not cover all losses we incur. In addition, $5.0 million of the purchase price was deposited into an escrow account as the sole source of recovery for post-closing purchase price adjustments. If we incur liabilities that are not covered by insurance or the escrow, we may bear the full cost, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.

We have recorded significant goodwill and other intangible assets in connection with the Captivate Acquisition, which could become impaired.

In connection with the Captivate Acquisition, we recorded $109.3 million of goodwill and $183.3 million of other intangible assets, including customer relationships, trade name, installed base and developed technology. We are required to test goodwill for impairment at least annually, and to test goodwill and other long-lived assets more frequently if events or changes in circumstances indicate that their carrying amount may not be recoverable. Declines in office occupancy, the loss of significant building locations or advertisers, a failure to achieve anticipated synergies, sustained declines in our market capitalization or other adverse changes in our business or in the markets in which Captivate operates could result in impairment charges, which could be material to our results of operations in the period recognized.

Risks Related to Our Indebtedness

The substantial indebtedness of NCM LLC and Captivate could adversely affect our financial condition, limit our flexibility in operating our business and prevent us from fulfilling our obligations.

On September 18, 2026, in connection with the Captivate Acquisition, NCM Holdings, LLC, NCM LLC, Captivate Holdings, LLC and Captivate, LLC, as borrowers, entered into a credit agreement (the “2026 Credit Agreement”) with Crestline Direct Finance, L.P., as administrative agent and collateral agent, and the lenders party thereto. The 2026 Credit Agreement provides for a $275.0 million senior secured first lien term loan facility (the “2026 Term Loan Facility”) and a $25.0 million senior secured revolving credit facility (the “2026 Revolving Credit Facility” and, together with the 2026 Term Loan Facility, the “2026 Credit Facilities”), each maturing on September 18, 2031. We used borrowings under the 2026 Credit Facilities, together with cash on hand, to fund the Captivate Acquisition, to repay in full and terminate the 2025 Credit Facility and to pay related fees and expenses. As of October 1, 2026, we had approximately $285.0 million of indebtedness outstanding under the 2026 Credit Facilities, consisting of $275.0 million under the 2026 Term Loan Facility and $10.0 million under the 2026 Revolving Credit Facility. Our total net leverage ratio, as defined in the 2026 Credit Agreement, was 4.38 to 1.00 as of October 1, 2026.

If the Company is unable to meet its debt service obligations, comply with the financial maintenance covenants, or the other restrictive affirmative and negative covenants that, among other things, limit our ability to incur additional indebtedness, grant liens, make investments and acquisitions, merge or consolidate, dispose of assets, pay dividends and make other distributions, prepay subordinated indebtedness and enter into transactions with affiliates, then we could be forced to restructure or refinance the obligations, seek additional equity financing or sell assets. This would also restrict our ability to receive distributions, to make other investments in the business, and result in other negative consequences. This substantial indebtedness could also have other important consequences, including:

•
requiring us to dedicate a substantial portion of the cash flow from operations of NCM LLC and Captivate to the payment of principal and interest, including scheduled quarterly amortization of the 2026 Term Loan Facility equal to 2.5% per annum of its original principal amount for the first three years and 5.0% per annum thereafter, and mandatory prepayments from a percentage of our excess cash flow. This reduces the funds available for working capital, capital expenditures, investments in our digital and digital out-of-home strategy, acquisitions, and dividends and share repurchases;
•
limiting our ability to obtain financing in the future;
•
limiting our liquidity and operational flexibility in changing economic, business and competitive conditions, which could require us to defer planned capital expenditures, reduce discretionary spending, sell assets, restructure existing debt or defer acquisitions or other strategic opportunities;
•
making us more vulnerable to increases in interest rates, declines in theater attendance or office occupancy, a downturn in operating performance or a decline in general economic conditions; and
•
limiting our ability to pay dividends or repurchase our common stock. In connection with the Captivate Acquisition, we paused our quarterly dividend and our share repurchase program, and we intend to prioritize the use of free cash flow to reduce our indebtedness. There can be no assurance as to whether or when we will resume paying dividends or repurchasing shares.

The restrictions and covenants in the 2026 Credit Agreement may also prevent us from taking actions that we believe would help us grow our business or respond to changes in market conditions, including pursuing acquisitions, investing in new advertising products or returning capital to our stockholders. Subject to any applicable cure periods, a breach of any covenants, a failure to make

 

37

 

required payments, a change of control or the occurrence of an event of default under the 2026 Credit Agreement could permit the lenders to declare all outstanding amounts immediately due and payable under the 2026 Credit Agreement and to terminate their commitments under the 2026 Revolving Credit Facility. If our indebtedness were accelerated, we might not have sufficient cash, or be able to obtain financing, to repay it. Obtaining a waiver of, or an amendment to, the covenants could require us to pay significant fees, accept higher interest rates or agree to more restrictive terms.
